‍<strong>En Égypte, des centaines de mil: In Egypt, hundreds of activists, including several Canadians, have been arbitrarily detained since yesterday. Roughly 4,000 people from 84 countries gathered in Cairo for the Global March to Gaza, a peaceful initiative led by the civilian, apolitical movement of the same name. The mobilization aims to denounce the blockade, the famine and the ongoing genocide in Gaza. What is the situation on the ground, and why is Egypt obstructing this citizen-led initiative? We spoke with activists, a journalist on the ground and a Middle East expert to better understand what is happening.
« Une personne a été séparée du groupe [: “One person was separated from the [Canadian] group at a checkpoint, and we haven't had any news of them for almost 7 hours. Their wife, who is also there, is panicking!” Tatiana Harker, vice-president of the Canadian delegation for the Global March to Gaza, told us.
Une centaine de Canadiens se sont joints: About a hundred Canadians joined the initiative. But on the ground, some sixty of them were arbitrarily detained, and their passports were confiscated. “Six members of the delegation were kidnapped in the city of Al-Arish, then released later. Some others were released in the middle of nowhere...” Harker adds. Some delegation members were intercepted directly in their hotels, which raises questions about the surveillance carried out by the authorities.
Initialement, les délégations devaient a: The delegations were initially supposed to arrive in Cairo between June 11 and 12. On June 13, a bus departure was planned for Al-Arish, a city in the Sinai Peninsula, about 350 kilometres east of the capital. From Al-Arish, the activists were to begin a 48-kilometre march toward Rafah, at the border with Gaza. The goal: to maintain symbolic pressure on the Egyptian authorities to open the crossing to humanitarian aid.
« [Les autorités égyptiennes] ont fait m: “[The Egyptian authorities] forced people onto the buses, they hit some of them, they took others. (...) As soon as people were filming, [they] tried to grab the phones, steal them, smash them on the ground,” says Lucy Davalou, a freelance journalist who was herself stuck on a bus held by the Egyptian police.
« L’État égyptien (...) est connu pour s: “The Egyptian state (...) is known for its authoritarian power (...),” explains Sami Aoun, Director of the Observatory on the Middle East and North Africa at the Université de Sherbrooke. “This regime is very suspicious of any mobilization within its civil society or in the diasporas, where it [fears] a certain influence from the Muslim Brotherhood or other liberal democratic currents.”
D’autre part, le pays a signé des accord: In addition, the country has signed peace agreements with Israel and does not want to be “challenged on this point,” the researcher points out. “[The Egyptian authorities see] in any demonstration the freedom of groups, NGOs, people who accuse it of a certain cowardice or a certain complicity with Israel.”
Or, cette marche visait à mettre en lumi: Yet this march was meant to shed light on the genocidal situation in Gaza, Harker reminds us. She therefore laments that “media attention is being diverted away from Gaza.”
Il est près de 21h à Montréal, 5 heures: It is nearly 9 p.m. in Montréal, 5 a.m. in Egypt. Hundreds of demonstrators may spend an entire night on buses, waiting to be sent back to their countries. Earlier in the night, videos of them reached us. Together, they are singing chants for the liberation of Palestine. In Montréal, a demonstration is relaying their voices in front of the Egyptian consulate.
En Libye, un millier de manifestants ven: In Libya, a thousand demonstrators who came from Mauritania, Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia to join Rafah are, for their part, stuck in the east of the country.
